title: Hunting with fire

names.note: Also 'firewood'; baya wayu is 'light a fire'.

identification.basis: The dictionary has no single word for a fire drive. It does have ngalku 'bush fire', duli 'burnt patch of grass', balbi 'hunt for', kangal 'chase' and the wallaby and kangaroo names. The drive itself is documented for the Kuku Yalanji of the Bloomfield River by Anderson (1996), drawing on Kuku Yalanji teachers and on Le Souef (1894) and Hodgkinson (1886).

summary: Kuku Yalanji hunting on land was usually a matter of one or two men, but in the dry season whole groups held **wallaby drives with fire**. Fires were 'carefully lit to create a ‘wall’ of fire going in one direction with only a few openings'. Young people walked in a long line through the bush, beating it and shouting, and the kangaroos and [wallabies](entry:wallaby) ran for the gaps, where older men waited with spears [ref:anderson1996]. The dictionary's **ngalku** is 'bush fire' and **duli** 'burnt patch of grass' [ref:hershberger1982]. Fire is now regulated. On some Western Yalanji determination areas native title expressly excludes lighting fires for hunting [ref:brady2013]. [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) is under a different, 1998 determination, so people there should ask the Traditional Owners and the station.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **Ngalku** is 'bush fire' and **duli** is 'burnt patch of grass'. Fire is **baya** or **kunjin**, and *baya wayu* is 'light a fire'. **Kubu** is smoke [ref:hershberger1982]. The hunter's words are **balbi** 'hunt for, search for', **kangal** 'chase', **karangaji** 'stalk' and **mala-minya** 'good hunter' [ref:hershberger1982]. The fire drill is **jimal**, Roth's Bloomfield *tchi-mal* [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904]. The game includes **kadar** 'plains wallaby', **darrba** 'grass wallaby' and the grey kangaroos **julmbanu** and **mayarriji** [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
**Bloomfield River (Kuku Yalanji).** Anderson describes the dry-season drives as the big exception to solitary hunting. They 'involved both young and old men, and occasionally women'. The fires made a wall moving one way, with a few openings left. The young people started inside a forested area and drove the animals toward the openings, where the older men waited with [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:anderson1996].

**Neighbours, as Roth recorded them** [ref:roth1901]:

- **Cape Bedford** (Guugu Yimithirr, to the north): the whole camp lit 'a long line of bush-fires — up to a mile long — extending to the summit of some hill if possible'. The men formed a line and circled round, spearing the kangaroos caught between them and the fires.
- **Pennefather River** (west Cape York): 'a three-quarter circle of fires' was lit, and the best spear-throwers watched the gap between its two ends.
- **Endeavour River**: Cook noted that people could be traced 'by the fires which they kindled in their way', and that kangaroos were so afraid of fire that the ship's dogs could hardly force them over newly burnt ground.
- **Atherton**: big kangaroo [nets](entry:nets) of kurrajong-fibre twine (see [string and twine](entry:string-and-twine)) were set across tracks to water, and hunters drove animals into them by shouting. Roth does not mention fire there.

Roth thought the systematic grass burning Leichhardt saw in the Burdekin and Gulf country was probably linked to fire drives [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Where and on what country
sections.body:
Drives need grassy open forest that will carry fire. On the upper Mitchell that is the ironbark and box woodland of the ridges. Cullen's ironbark and Molloy red box are among the woodland trees recorded around Karma Waters [ref:ala-karma]. The Queensland Herbarium's guideline for this kind of woodland on the Einasleigh Uplands calls for early-dry-season and storm-time burns, 'low, with occasional moderate' intensity, at 2–5 year intervals. It says to burn less than 40% of the landscape in any year and to leave long-unburnt patches 'to maintain a diversity of habitat for wildlife' [ref:re-woodland].

The paperbark fringe along the river is different. The guideline for it says 'do not burn deliberately', and lets fire only trickle in from the woodland [ref:re9314].

Karma Waters itself burns 'most of our country' on a three-to-four-year cycle, depending on the seasons, to clear excess fuel and control weeds [ref:kw-land]. The Western Yalanji say their country has 'suffered from wildfires since traditional burning practices all but ceased in the 20th century', and have begun a savanna burning project [ref:wyac2020].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body:
The Bloomfield drives were held in the dry season [ref:anderson1996]. On Cape York, the early dry, as the grass starts to cure, gives low-severity fires. By the late dry, fuels are completely dry and fires can be severe and widespread. Storm burns are lit after the first storm rains, normally between October and January [ref:pbg-cape-york]. At Palmerville, the nearest long weather record to Karma Waters, bad fire-weather days average about 36 °C with about 18% humidity [ref:pbg-cape-york].

Down the Mitchell at Kowanyama (Kokoberra, Yir Yoront and Kunjen country), Traditional Owner Clarita Yam describes the early burn as 'after the wet when the grass is [mostly] still green'. She adds that 'when you burn too much, you burn out your Country and there's nothing left for your cattle, wallabies and kangaroo' [ref:kowanyama2024].

sections.heading: What fire did for the hunt
sections.body:
- **Driving game.** A line or arc of fire moved animals toward waiting hunters [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901].
- **Opening the country.** In the Western Desert, Martu hunters burn small patches of country to expose sand goanna burrows. Their small fires leave a fine mosaic of burnt and regrowing country [ref:bird2008]. That is a desert people's practice. We found no published Kuku Yalanji record of burning for [goannas](entry:goanna).
- **Looking after country.** Eastern Kuku Yalanji used cultural burning 'to help maintain the health of the land for thousands of years' [ref:newsport].

sections.heading: How a Bloomfield drive was run
sections.body:
This is a record of the old method from Anderson's account [ref:anderson1996], not instructions. It is not lawful for most people today (see *On Country today*).

1. **Choose the time and place.** It must be the dry season, on grassy forest country where the animals are known to be.
2. **Bring fire.** Men carried [firesticks](entry:firestick) wrapped in [paperbark](entry:paperbark) in their bags [ref:anderson1996].
3. **Set the waiting line.** The older men, the best spearmen, take up positions at the planned gaps.
4. **Light the fire carefully** so that it forms a wall moving in one direction, leaving only a few openings.
5. **Beat the bush.** Starting inside the forest, the young people walk in a long line, beating and shouting.
6. **Spear at the gaps** as kangaroos, wallabies and smaller animals come through.
7. **Cook the game.** Wallabies were usually cooked straight on the fire after the bones were broken with an axe [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body: A grass fire can outrun a person, especially on late-dry days of heat, low humidity and wind [ref:pbg-cape-york]. In Queensland, occupiers must take all reasonable steps to control or put out a fire on their land, warn neighbours and call 000 [ref:qfes-pp]. Lighting fires to hunt also puts cattle, fences and other people at risk.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**Queensland law.** A fire smaller than 2 metres in every dimension may be lit without a permit if adequate precautions are taken. A larger fire needs a Permit to Light Fire from the local Fire Warden, and no fire may be lit during a fire ban [ref:qfd]. Permits are free, and the occupier is responsible for any fire on their land [ref:qfes-pp].

**Native title: which determination says what.**

- The **2013 Western Yalanji determinations** (#4, [2013] FCA 958, and the combined #5 and #7) cover country around the Palmer and Mitchell north-west of Mount Carbine. Their fire right is to 'light fires on the area for domestic purposes including cooking, but not for the purpose of hunting or clearing vegetation' [ref:brady2013] [ref:wyac2020].
- The **2026 Western Yalanji determination** allows fires 'for cultural, spiritual or domestic purposes including cooking, but not for the purpose of hunting or clearing vegetation' [ref:fca2026wy].
- **Karma Waters** falls under neither. It is under the **1998 *Western Yalanji or 'Sunset' Peoples v Pedersen*** consent determination [ref:kw-about] [ref:wyac2020]. Its published summary recognises rights to use the area and its natural resources for 'social, cultural, economic, religious, spiritual, customary and traditional purposes'. It says nothing about fire either way [ref:wyac2020]. We have not seen the full 1998 orders.

Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* protects native title holders' hunting for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs from licence and permit requirements [ref:alrc].

**At Karma Waters**, visitors' campfires are restricted to the campsite, and weapons and hunting dogs are not allowed [ref:kw-induction]. Anyone who wants to burn country, or to learn about fire, should ask the Western Yalanji Traditional Owners (through the Western Yalanji Aboriginal Corporation in Mareeba) and the station first [ref:wyac2020].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: **Nyunil** 'extinguish, or to put a fire or light out'; **miyilkura** 'smouldering log'; **ngunjil** 'charcoal; hot coals or hot ashes'; **jakalambal** 'start a fire, start to cook food' [ref:hershberger1982].
